analysis.one_liner: Gives federal food regulators authority to order recalls and fine companies that ship unsafe meat, poultry, and food.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: after introduction it was referred to two House committees and sat in subcommittees until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone in the food business that suspects its products are unsafe to tell the Agriculture Department. It would let regulators stop distribution, force a recall when companies will not act voluntarily, pull federal inspectors out of repeat-offender plants, and fine violators up to $100,000 per violation per day for meat and poultry, and up to $500,000 for food companies. Today, meat and poultry recalls are technically voluntary, and food companies can ship adulterated products without facing civil fines.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would get faster warnings and recalls of contaminated meat, poultry, and packaged food, and would be protected by real fines instead of relying on companies to recall products on their own [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of meat, poultry, and packaged food

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires any business (other than a household consumer) that has reason to believe its meat, poultry, or food is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of Agriculture, closing the gap where contaminated products could quietly stay in commerce [S2][S3].

It gives the Secretary authority to stop distribution and, after a short hearing within two business days, order a mandatory recall where a company fails to act voluntarily, plus direct notice to affected consumers [S3].
It lets the Agriculture Department withdraw or refuse federal inspection from plants with willful or repeated violations, which stops those plants from shipping meat or poultry at all [S3].

It creates civil penalties — up to $100,000 per violation per day for meat and poultry violations, and up to $500,000 for companies (or $100,000 for individuals) for unsafe food — giving regulators a real financial deterrent instead of the few enforcement tools then available [S3].

The CRS summary confirms the bill added notification requirements and authority for nondistribution, recall, withdrawal of inspectors, and civil penalties across the meat, poultry, and food laws [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors, food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers, who would bear the cost of mandatory recalls, record-keeping for regulators, and civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation per day; some of these costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices [S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: companies of every size would have to monitor their products for problems, maintain distribution records for the government, and execute recalls quickly, and smaller firms with thinner margins would feel these costs most [S3].

The bill gives the Agriculture Secretary broad discretion — including penalties in lieu of prosecution and wide power to decide what a recall requires — which industry groups typically argued invites overreach and inconsistent enforcement, though the bill does include hearings and judicial review to check agency decisions [S3].
Some recall costs, particularly for perishable products pulled on imperfect information, would eventually show up in consumer prices, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a modest, predictable cost to food companies for a large public benefit: mandatory recall authority and meaningful fines in a system where contaminated meat could previously be recalled only if the company agreed. The checks built into the bill (two-day hearings, judicial review, penalties scaled to business size) addressed the main overreach objection. The bill was never debated, so those tradeoffs were never tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees and their subcommittees in late 2003, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2003, by Rep. Diana DeGette, joined on introduction by Reps. DeLauro, Hinchey, Stark, and Waxman [S3].
It was referred to two committees — Agriculture and Energy and Commerce — meaning two different committees each had to act before the bill could move [S5].

In early December 2003 it was referred to the Agriculture subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture and the Energy and Commerce subcommittee on Health; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed [S5].
The bill finished with 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, with the bill still in committee [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors and food manufacturers came out ahead: without the bill becoming law, recalls stayed voluntary, inspectors could not be pulled from violating plants under this framework, and no per-day civil penalties applied. Consumers got none of the protections it offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors, food manufacturers

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill died without any hearing or vote in committees controlled by Republicans, so the record shows a Democratic-backed bill with no Republican support that never advanced [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would subject them to mandatory recall orders, possible loss of federal inspectors, and civil fines up to $100,000 per violation per day [S3]. Their cost would come directly from keeping adulterated meat and poultry away from consumers [S2][S3].

Under the food provisions, retailers and distributors as well as manufacturers would be required to notify regulators of suspect food, cease distribution, and face penalties up to $500,000 per act per day for companies [S3].

Retailers are included in the notification and cease-distribution duties, but they also benefit when mandatory recall authority clears contaminated products off shelves faster, protecting them from selling unsafe goods [S3].
